verses.text: After we made it safely to shore, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us extraordinary kindness. They lit a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire. A viper, driven out by the heat, latched onto his hand.
When the local people saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to each other, “This man must be a murderer. He escaped the sea, but Justice won’t let him live.”
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and wasn’t harmed.
They expected him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. After waiting a long time and seeing nothing happen, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Nearby were lands owned by the island’s leading man, named Publius. He welcomed us and kindly hosted us for three days.
Publius’ father was sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After that happened, the rest of the sick people on the island also came and were healed.
They honored us in many ways, and when we sailed, they supplied everything we needed.
After three months, we sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island. Its figurehead showed the Twin Brothers.
We stopped at Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
From there we sailed around the coast and reached Rhegium. The next day a south wind came up, and two days later we arrived at Puteoli,
where we found believers who invited us to stay with them for seven days. Then we went on to Rome.
The believers there had heard about us and came to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. The other prisoners were handed over to the captain of the guard.

Three days later, Paul called together the Jewish leaders. When they arrived, he said, “Brothers, I haven’t done anything against our people or the customs of our ancestors. Yet I was handed over as a prisoner in Jerusalem to the Romans,
who examined me and wanted to release me because they found nothing deserving death.
But when the Jews objected, I had to appeal to Caesar—not because I had any charge against my own people.
That’s why I asked to see you and talk with you. I’m wearing this chain because of Israel’s hope.”
They said to him, “We haven’t received any letters from Judea about you, and none of our people who have come here has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we’d like to hear what you think. We know this group is spoken against everywhere.”

They set a day to meet with him, and many people came to where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained God’s Kingdom and tried to persuade them about Jesus, using the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were convinced by what he said, but others didn’t believe.
They couldn’t agree with one another, and they began to leave after Paul made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah to your ancestors,
saying, ‘Go to this people and tell them: You will hear and hear, but never understand; you will look and look, but never see.

For this people’s heart has become dull. Their ears barely hear, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, turn back, and I would heal them.’”
“So let it be known to you: God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.”
After he said this, the Jews left, arguing strongly among themselves.
Paul stayed for two full years in a house he rented himself and welcomed everyone who came to him.
He preached God’s Kingdom and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without anyone stopping him.
